newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain to meet 2.5 pct deficit goal easily - Folgado. [CORRECTED 17:17 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Spain to meet 2.5 pct deficit goal easily - Folgado. [CORRECTED 17:17 GMT]

text.p: Spanish Budget Secretary Jose Folgado said on Wednesday that the central government would easily meet its 2.5 percent deficit to gross domestic product target this year without taking any further measures.
"We've done our forecasts. Both on a cash and on a national account basis we will easily meet the target (of 2.5 percent)," Folgado told Reuters in a telephone interview.

Earlier on Wednesday the Economy Ministry published June central government deficit data. The data showed the deficit standing at 1.7 percent of GDP for the first six months of the year versus 1.2 percent (corrects figure from 1.1 percent) in the January-May period.

To meet the Maastricht criteria of an overall public deficit to GDP ratio of three percent, Spain is forecasting a 2.5 percent deficit for the central government and a 0.5 percent deficit for both regional government and social security spending.
"The (central government deficit to GDP) will be at most 2.5 percent, and may even be lower," Folgado said.

The central government public deficit on a national account basis takes into account accrued revenues and expenditures for a given period, while the deficit on a cash basis registers actual money movements during a given month.

Folgado said that later this year the effect of the change in the accounting method from a cash basis to a national account basis for interest payments on short-term bills would imply a reduction in the deficit of around 240 billion pesetas ($1.6 billion).
"This adjustment will be some 300 billion pesetas for a full year. So far (to June) this adjustment has (impacted) as little as 62 billion pesetas," he said.

"The truth is that things are going very well and now it seems (the deficit) could also be lower (than 2.5 percent over GDP), but you can never be sure in advance, because there are always exceptional circumstances."
"This year we do not have the slightest worry about meeting the deficit (target). This time last year we were worried, but not now."
He added that revenues are performing well while spending is under control and the economy is picking up.
"(Value-added tax) revenues are higher than previously expected, and corporate tax receipts are doing fine as well," he said.
In June alone VAT receipts were down 2.8 percent, but in the first half they were up 7.8 percent.
He said the government had advanced some payments to regional governments and to state firms in the first half.
Folgado admitted that lower inflation, now targeted at 2.2 percent for year-end, implied reduced GDP growth in nominal terms -- 5.2 percent instead of 6.0 percent as forecast in the 1997 budget.
"This is causing some problems," he said.
But this did not change the global picture.

"Our calculations show (the deficit to GDP) will be around 2.4 percent or 2.5 percent. It is more likely to be 2.5 percent. One year ago we needed some budget adjustments, but not this year," he added.
